title: If conserved in mammals, Vmem modulation offers cancer detection and treatment routes

fields.label: Label
fields.value: If conserved in mammals, Vmem modulation offers cancer detection and treatment routes

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The authors predict that if the role of remote endogenous bioelectric states in tumorigenesis is conserved in mammalian cancer models, modulation of resting membrane potential — potentially with ion channel drugs already approved for human use — would provide new cancer detection and treatment modalities.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Chernet BT 2014, Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range › DISCUSSION › Transducing hyperpolarization into cell responses: HDAC1 inhibition

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Future work must also examine the roles of remote endogenous bioelectric states in mammalian cancer models; if conserved, these data suggest a number of detection and treatment modalities focused on Vmem modulation.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Chernet BT, Levin M, “Transmembrane voltage potential of somatic cells controls oncogene-mediated tumorigenesis at long-range”, Oncotarget (2014), doi:10.18632/oncotarget.1935; section “DISCUSSION › Transducing hyperpolarization into cell responses: HDAC1 inhibition”. Scope: Mammalian cancer models and, by extension, human cancer therapy

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2014-tumor-12: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.41

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The translational prediction is measurable, but the source identifies mammalian testing as future work. Current public clinical and preclinical resources do not contain the required controlled remote-Vmem intervention and readouts.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In mammalian cancer models, manipulate remote tissue Vmem with clinically relevant ion-channel drugs and measure tumor initiation, progression, and detectable remote voltage signatures. Conservation would require effects at tolerated exposures across multiple models.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Approved-drug status does not imply suitability for Vmem modulation in tumors.

The claim is explicitly conditional on conservation in mammals.

Existing Xenopus results do not establish efficacy or detection performance in mammals.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.2
discriminating power: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.4
operationalizability: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.1

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction is conditional on conservation in mammalian models and on a therapeutic effect of voltage modulation. Channel-drug catalogs list candidate reagents and do not contain the remote-voltage experiments. Cancer genomics portals likewise lack this physiological exposure, so the conservation claim still requires new mammalian data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In mammalian tumor models, change resting potential of host tissue remote from the tumor, preferably with clinically used channel drugs, and test detection and tumor-growth endpoints against voltage-clamped controls. Conservation would appear as a remote-voltage effect on detection or growth; its absence in adequately powered models would refute conservation.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Approved channel drugs have extensive non-voltage pharmacology, so a clinical association would not identify the Xenopus mechanism.

Mammalian studies do not publicly pair remote host Vmem with tumor incidence under these interventions.
